4 marks: (a) Any four, 1 mark each: reliable supply of good quality water; soil with high clay content to hold water; gently sloping topography for drainage; freedom from flooding; accessibility to market and roads; security; nearness to source of fingerlings and feed
8 marks: (b) Any four, 2 marks each: regular feeding with appropriate quantity of quality feed; monitoring water quality (pH, oxygen, temperature) and changing water; fertilising/liming to maintain plankton; controlling weeds and predators; preventing and treating diseases; regular sampling to check growth; repairing dykes and screens; record keeping
6 marks: (c) Any two, 3 marks each: smoking - gutted fish arranged in a smoking kiln over a slow fire until dry, reduces moisture and smoke compounds inhibit microbes; salting - fish soaked in brine or packed in dry salt, draws water out; sun-drying - spread on racks in the sun; freezing - stored at very low temperatures to stop microbial activity; canning - cooked and sealed in sterilised airtight cans
questions.explanation: (a) A pond site needs reliable good water, clay soil that retains water, gentle slope, no flooding, good access, security and nearness to inputs. (b) After stocking the farmer feeds the fish regularly, monitors and maintains water quality, fertilises and limes, controls weeds and predators, treats diseases and samples growth. (c) Smoking dries fish over a slow fire in a kiln; salting draws out water and inhibits bacteria; freezing stops microbial activity.

questions.stem:
(a) State the law of demand and the law of supply. [4 marks]
(b) Explain four factors that affect the demand for an agricultural product. [8 marks]
(c) The price of a crate of eggs rose from ₦3 000 to ₦3 600 and the quantity demanded fell from 500 crates to 350 crates. Calculate the price elasticity of demand and state whether demand is elastic or inelastic. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Law of demand: other things being equal, the higher the price, the lower the quantity demanded, and vice versa
2 marks: (a) Law of supply: other things being equal, the higher the price, the higher the quantity supplied, and vice versa
8 marks: (b) Any four, 2 marks each: price of the commodity; income of consumers; prices of substitutes and complements; taste and fashion; population size; season; government policy (taxes/subsidies); expectation of future price changes; advertisement
2 marks: (c) Percentage change in quantity = (500 - 350)/500 x 100 = 30%
2 marks: (c) Percentage change in price = (3600 - 3000)/3000 x 100 = 20%
1 mark: (c) Elasticity = 30/20 = 1.5
1 mark: (c) Demand is elastic (elasticity greater than 1)
questions.explanation: (a) Demand falls as price rises; supply rises as price rises, other things being equal. (b) Demand depends on price, income, prices of substitutes and complements, taste, population, season and expectations. (c) Quantity fell by 30% and price rose by 20%, so elasticity = 30/20 = 1.5, which is elastic.

questions.stem:
(a) State four reasons for keeping farm records. [4 marks]
(b) Name four types of farm records and state the information found in each. [8 marks]
(c) A farmer bought a planter for ₦1 500 000. It has a useful life of 5 years and a salvage value of ₦250 000. Using the straight-line method, calculate the annual depreciation and the book value at the end of the third year. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: (a) Any four, 1 mark each: to know profit or loss; to plan future operations; to obtain loans; for tax assessment; to settle disputes; to monitor performance of enterprises; for inheritance purposes
8 marks: (b) Any four, 2 marks each: inventory - list and value of farm assets; farm diary - daily activities and events; production records - yields of crops, eggs, milk, births; sales/purchase records - items sold or bought, quantities and prices; payroll - names of workers and wages; feeding records; health/vaccination records; input records
1 mark: (c) Annual depreciation = (cost - salvage value)/useful life
2 marks: (c) = (1 500 000 - 250 000)/5 = ₦250 000 per year
1 mark: (c) Accumulated depreciation after 3 years = 3 x 250 000 = ₦750 000
2 marks: (c) Book value at end of year 3 = 1 500 000 - 750 000 = ₦750 000
questions.explanation: (a) Records show profit or loss, aid planning, support loan applications and taxation, and help settle disputes. (b) Inventory lists assets; the farm diary records daily activities; production records show yields; sales and purchase records show transactions; payroll records wages. (c) Depreciation = (1 500 000 - 250 000)/5 = ₦250 000 per year; book value after 3 years = 1 500 000 - 750 000 = ₦750 000.

questions.stem:
(a) Define marketing of agricultural produce. [2 marks]
(b) Explain five functions of marketing. [10 marks]
(c) State three problems of marketing agricultural produce in West Africa and one solution to each. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) All the activities involved in moving farm produce from the producer to the final consumer, including assembling, processing, storage, transport and selling
10 marks: (b) Any five, 2 marks each: assembling - collecting produce from many farmers; grading and standardisation - sorting by quality/size; processing - changing form to add value and reduce perishability; storage - keeping produce until needed, stabilising supply; transportation - moving produce to markets; packaging; financing; risk bearing; advertising/selling; market information
6 marks: (c) Any three problems + solutions, 2 marks each: poor storage facilities - build silos/cold stores; bad roads - construct feeder roads; price fluctuation - guaranteed minimum prices/storage; exploitation by middlemen - cooperative marketing; perishability - processing; lack of market information - extension/ICT price information; inadequate grading - standard grading
questions.explanation: (a) Marketing covers all activities moving produce from farm to consumer. (b) Assembling, grading, processing, storage and transport ensure produce reaches consumers in the right form, place and time. (c) Poor storage can be solved by silos and cold rooms, bad roads by feeder roads, price swings by guaranteed prices, middlemen exploitation by cooperatives and perishability by processing.

questions.stem:
(a) What is agricultural extension? [2 marks]
(b) Describe three methods of agricultural extension, one each for individual, group and mass contact. [9 marks]
(c) State four problems of agricultural extension in Nigeria and suggest a solution to each. [7 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) The process of educating farmers on improved farming practices and passing farmers' problems to research institutions for solutions
3 marks: (b) Individual method, e.g. farm and home visits / office calls / personal letters - extension agent meets the farmer to give specific advice
3 marks: (b) Group method, e.g. method or result demonstrations / field days / meetings / tours - shows a practice to many farmers at once
3 marks: (b) Mass method, e.g. radio, television, newspapers, posters, mobile phone messages - reaches large numbers quickly
4 marks: (c) Problems, any four, 1 mark each: inadequate number of extension agents; poor funding; poor transport/mobility; illiteracy of farmers; language barriers; poor communication between research and farmers; insecurity in rural areas
3 marks: (c) Solutions (any three matched, 1 mark each): recruit and train more agents; increase funding; provide vehicles/motorcycles; adult education; use local languages; strengthen research-extension linkage; use ICT/mobile phones
questions.explanation: (a) Extension educates farmers on improved practices and relays their problems to research. (b) Farm visits give individual advice; demonstrations and field days reach groups; radio, TV and SMS reach the masses. (c) Problems include too few agents, poor funding, lack of transport, illiteracy and weak research links; solutions are recruiting and training agents, more funding, vehicles, adult education, local languages and ICT.

questions.stem:
(a) Name the four factors of production and state the reward for each. [8 marks]
(b) Explain four ways by which the efficiency of labour on a farm can be improved. [8 marks]
(c) State two characteristics of land as a factor of production. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Land - rent
2 marks: (a) Labour - wages/salaries
2 marks: (a) Capital - interest
2 marks: (a) Entrepreneur/management - profit
8 marks: (b) Any four, 2 marks each: training and education of workers; adequate and prompt payment/incentives; good working conditions and welfare (housing, health care); provision of improved tools and machines; division of labour/specialisation; good supervision and management; adequate nutrition
2 marks: (c) Any two, 1 mark each: fixed in supply; immobile; subject to diminishing returns; varies in fertility and location; a free gift of nature
questions.explanation: (a) Land earns rent, labour earns wages, capital earns interest and the entrepreneur earns profit. (b) Labour efficiency improves with training, good pay and incentives, better welfare, improved tools, specialisation and good supervision. (c) Land is fixed in supply and immobile.
